resources.string: ActuA11y demonstrates accessibility patterns in readable source code. Each topic has two versions, switched with the toggle in the app bar: a Naive version built without accessibility in mind, and a Better version built with it. Naive versions are deliberately flawed — if one feels broken, that is the point, not a bug in this app.\n\nIf you use TalkBack, switch access, or a keyboard, try both versions of a topic and compare.
Learn how to use TalkBack (opens Android\'s official documentation)
Images and icon buttons need descriptions so TalkBack can read them aloud.
Turn on TalkBack and swipe through the examples below. Note what — if anything — is announced for each one, then switch versions with the toggle in the app bar and compare.
A smartphone icon representing a mobile device

For meaningful images, pass a non-null string to the Image contentDescription parameter — TalkBack reads it when the image is focused. For decorative images, pass null; Compose removes the node from the accessibility tree entirely.

For icon-only buttons, set contentDescription on the Icon inside IconButton. This is the only name TalkBack has for that button.

See: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties

Neither the meaningful image nor the icon button carries a contentDescription. Compose's Image only adds a semantics node when contentDescription is non-null, so the meaningful image here carries none at all — TalkBack has nothing to focus and skips it silently, indistinguishable from a genuinely decorative image. The IconButton is still a real clickable node, so TalkBack does focus it, but with no name for what it does.

The decorative image is unchanged from the Better version — a decorative image is correctly null in both, so there is nothing to contrast on that element specifically.

See the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties

TalkBack normally reads elements in roughly the order they appear on screen, top to bottom. But when elements overlap — a button floating over the corner of a list, for example — that raw ordering can get confusing, jumping between areas in a way that does not match what the screen looks like.

Turn on TalkBack and swipe through the list and the round button over its corner below. Note the order things are announced in — does it finish the list before reaching the button, or does the button interrupt partway through? Then switch versions with the toggle in the app bar and compare.

The list above carries Modifier.semantics { isTraversalGroup = true }. TalkBack's swipe order is computed by sorting the accessibility tree geometrically, banding nodes into rows by screen position. Where a floating element's bounds overlap another region — as the button here overlaps the list's last row — that geometric sort can interleave the two unless one of them is marked as an atomic group. isTraversalGroup tells the sort to treat this list as a single unit: its own children are still ordered normally within it, but from the outside it behaves as one node relative to the button.

older articles and answers describe this same idea under the name isContainer. That API still compiles today — it is only @Deprecated, not removed — but it is a dead stub: Compose's traversal sort reads only SemanticsProperties.IsTraversalGroup and never looks at IsContainer, so code still using isContainer has no effect on TalkBack ordering even though it builds without error.

See: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties.IsTraversalGroup

This list carries no isTraversalGroup, so its rows and the overlapping button are sorted together in a single geometric pass, the same pass used for any sibling whose bounds intersect it.

TODO(verify): confirm on a real device whether TalkBack actually interleaves the button between list rows in swipe order for this exact layout, and record the Compose BOM version and API level tested.

See the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties.IsTraversalGroup

Within a group, TalkBack normally reads elements left to right, top to bottom. Sometimes the visual order and the sensible reading order disagree — a dismiss button placed in the top-left corner of a card, for example, usually should not be the first thing announced.
Turn on TalkBack and swipe through the card header below. Note whether the title or the dismiss button is announced first, then switch versions with the toggle in the app bar and compare.
Card header with a dismiss button

Both elements in the header above carry an explicit Modifier.semantics { traversalIndex = … } — 0f on the title, 1f on the dismiss button — so the title sorts first regardless of the button sitting to its left on screen.

Crucially, the Row itself also carries isTraversalGroup = true. traversalIndex only reorders siblings within their nearest enclosing traversal group; without one, it has no effect at all. See the Naive version of this same screen, which sets the identical indices but omits the group.

See: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties.TraversalIndex

This header sets the exact same traversalIndex values as the Better version — 0f on the title, 1f on the dismiss button — but the enclosing Row is not marked isTraversalGroup. Per Compose's own documentation, traversalIndex only takes effect within an enclosing traversal group; without one it is silently ignored, and TalkBack falls back to raw left-to-right order, announcing the dismiss button before the title. Nothing here looks wrong when reading the code — the indices are set correctly — which is exactly what makes this mistake easy to miss.

TODO(verify): confirm on a real device that the dismiss button is announced before the title here, and that the Better version announces the title first, recording the Compose BOM version and API level tested.

See the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties.IsTraversalGroup

TalkBack users can jump directly between section headings on a screen, skipping everything in between — similar to how a sighted reader\'s eye jumps straight to bold section titles when skimming a page. That only works if a heading is actually marked as one; text that merely looks bold, with no underlying semantics, is invisible to that navigation mode.

Turn on TalkBack, switch its reading control to \"Headings\", and try jumping between the three section titles below. Then switch versions with the toggle in the app bar and compare — the text looks identical in both, but only one version can actually be jumped between.
Manage your sign-in details and linked accounts.
Choose which alerts you receive and how.
Control what data is shared and with whom.

Each section title above carries Modifier.semantics { heading() }, in addition to its bold titleMedium styling. TalkBack\'s \"Headings\" reading control uses exactly this property — not text size or font weight — to decide what counts as a heading, so a user in that mode can swipe directly between \"Account\", \"Notifications\", and \"Privacy\", skipping the body text under each.\n\nSee: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties.Heading

These section titles are styled identically to the Better version — same font, same weight, same size — but carry no heading() semantics. Visually they read as headings; to TalkBack's "Headings" navigation they do not exist at all, so a user in that mode finds nothing to jump between and has to fall back to swiping through every line of body text to find a section.

TODO(verify): confirm on a real device that TalkBack's Headings reading control finds zero stops on this screen, versus three on the Better version, recording the Compose BOM version and API level tested.

See the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties.Heading

A pane is a visually distinct portion of a screen — a tab\'s content area, the inside of an open drawer — that can change without a full screen navigation. TalkBack has no built-in way to notice a pane\'s content changed unless the app tells it, the same way it is told the screen\'s own name when a topic first opens.

Turn on TalkBack and switch between the two view options below. Note whether anything is announced when the content underneath changes, then switch versions with the toggle in the app bar and compare.
Total this month: 128 items processed, 3 flagged for review.

Processed: 128
Flagged: 3
Average handling time: 4.2 minutes
Last updated: today

The content pane below carries Modifier.semantics { paneTitle = … }, and that string changes to match whichever view is selected. Per Compose's own documentation, a pane is a visually distinct portion of a window whose appearance or content can change independently — accessibility services can only announce that a pane changed if the pane's title itself changes when its content does. Switching between Summary and Details here never navigates anywhere; the same composable stays on screen throughout.

Contrast this with the paneTitle already set on this screen's own root — that one announces the screen's name once, on arrival, like every topic in this app. This one is expected to fire again on every selection change, which is the distinction requirements draw between "pane titles" as its own topic and the paneTitle every screen already carries.

TODO(verify): confirm on a real device that TalkBack announces the new pane title each time the view switches, and record the Compose BOM version and API level tested.

See: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties.PaneTitle

This content pane switches between the same two views as the Better version, with identical layout and text — but it carries no paneTitle of its own, only the screen-level one set once when the topic first opened. TalkBack has no signal that the content underneath changed at all: no announcement, and focus does not move, so a user relying on TalkBack may not realize anything happened after tapping Summary or Details.

TODO(verify): confirm on a real device that TalkBack stays silent when switching views here, versus announcing the new pane title in the Better version, recording the Compose BOM version and API level tested.

See the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties.PaneTitle

When a picker or dialog closes, a sighted user\'s eyes naturally return to whatever opened it. TalkBack\'s focus does not do that on its own — once the picker\'s content disappears, focus has nowhere defined to go, and can land at the top of the screen or be lost entirely.

Turn on TalkBack, move focus to the button below, open the picker, choose a frequency, and notice where TalkBack\'s focus lands once the picker closes. Then switch versions with the toggle in the app bar and compare.

The button above carries Modifier.focusRequester(…), and a LaunchedEffect calls requestFocus() on it once the picker closes. Compose does not hand focus back to whatever opened a dialog on its own; without an explicit request, where focus goes next is undefined.

Getting that call to actually succeed took two extra steps not obvious from the API alone — confirmed by an instrumented test on a real device (Pixel 9 Pro, API 37, Compose BOM 2025.05.00), not merely reasoned about: (1) waiting for LocalWindowInfo.current.isWindowFocused, since the dialog is a separate platform Window and hands focus back to the Activity asynchronously; and (2), the less expected one, calling InputModeManager.requestInputMode(InputMode.Keyboard) first. A Button's click target uses Focusability.SystemDefined internally, which refuses requestFocus() outright whenever the platform's current input mode is Touch — the default on any touchscreen device, unaffected by whether TalkBack is running, since TalkBack's own swipe gestures are still touch events. Skip that call and requestFocus() silently returns false with no exception, every time, regardless of the window-focus wait.

TODO(verify): confirm on a real device that TalkBack's own accessibility-focus cursor actually follows this button back after the picker closes — Compose's Focused state and TalkBack's cursor are related but distinct, and only the former is what this developer note and its instrumented test can confirm without TalkBack running. Record the Compose BOM version and API level tested.

See: androidx.compose.ui.focus.FocusRequester, androidx.compose.ui.focus.Focusability, androidx.compose.ui.input.InputModeManager

This picker opens and closes exactly like the Better version — same dialog, same options, same button — but the button never requests focus back afterwards. Once the picker's content leaves the tree, nothing tells Compose's focus system where to go next, so the outcome is undefined by this code; a TalkBack user has no guarantee of returning to where they were and may need to re-explore the screen from scratch.

TODO(verify): confirm on a real device where TalkBack's focus actually lands after closing this picker here, compared with the Better version, and record the Compose BOM version and API level tested.

See the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.ui.focus.FocusRequester

Some apps show a short numeric code — a PIN — as a row of boxes rather than a plain text field, with a button to reveal or hide what you\'ve typed. Getting that right for someone using a screen reader is trickier than it looks.

Turn on TalkBack. Enter a PIN below, then use the show/hide control. Listen for what — if anything — is announced when you toggle it, and check what actions TalkBack offers when you explore the field itself.

The naive version renders the PIN as six separate text fields and swaps each box's literal displayed text between the digit and a bullet character to fake masking. This version instead binds one BasicSecureTextField (androidx.compose.foundation.text, stable since Compose Foundation 1.8) to a single TextFieldState, decorated to draw the same six-box appearance around it. TalkBack now has exactly one field to explain and edit, not six — and only one set of text-editing actions, not six repeated copies of it.

BasicSecureTextField unconditionally marks its semantics node isPassword = true and sets contentType = ContentType.Password — confirmed by reading BasicSecureTextField.kt directly, not assumed from its name. isPassword is the same marker Android's accessibility API exposes as AccessibilityNodeInfo.isPassword, and contentType is what lets a password manager's autofill offer to fill this field at all — neither happens automatically on a hand-built field of plain text boxes, regardless of how it looks.

The show/hide control is a Modifier.toggleable(role = Role.Switch) with an explicit stateDescription ("PIN hidden" / "PIN visible"), not a button whose own label swaps between "Show" and "Hide". That is deliberate: state belongs on the control that owns it, announced the way TalkBack expects a two-state control to announce itself, rather than depending on whatever event the field happens to fire when its displayed value changes underneath it.

That said, this is not a fully solved problem. Confirmed by reading Compose's own event-dispatch code (AndroidComposeViewAccessibilityDelegateCompat.android.kt): Compose only suppresses the text-change announcement automatically when a field's isPassword flag itself flips between true and false (bug b/247891690). This field's isPassword stays true throughout — only its TextObfuscationMode changes — so that particular guard does not apply here, and toggling reveal may still surface a text-change event carrying the real value. TODO(verify): confirm on a real device — record TalkBack version, vendor, and whether the system's "speak passwords" setting is on — whether toggling reveal here is audibly silent, masked, or leaks the PIN through the change event regardless of the isPassword marker. The source only tells us what event Compose dispatches, not what TalkBack does with it.

The field still exposes standard text-editing actions (move cursor, select text) inherited from being a real editable field. Whether those make sense on a fixed-length numeric code is a separate, still-open question.

See: androidx.compose.foundation.text.BasicSecureTextField, androidx.compose.foundation.text.input.TextObfuscationMode, androidx.compose.ui.autofill.ContentType, androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties.Password

Each digit lives in its own text field — six separate focusable, editable elements for what is conceptually one six-digit value. TalkBack has to be swiped through all six individually just to reach or review the PIN, and each one exposes a full text-editing action set (select all, move cursor, cut, copy, paste) that makes little sense for a single character.

None of the six carries Password semantics. Masking here is done by hand: each box's actual displayed text is swapped between the digit and a bullet character, rather than using the framework's own password mechanism (isPassword, which the classic TextField derives automatically from PasswordVisualTransformation — confirmed by reading CoreTextField.kt). Because these fields never carry that marker, TalkBack has no signal this is sensitive content at all, and a password manager's autofill has nothing to attach to either.

The show/hide control's own label swaps between "Show PIN" and "Hide PIN" to communicate state, rather than using a control TalkBack recognises as a two-state toggle. And because each box's displayed text is what actually changes when you toggle it — real digits replacing bullet characters, or the reverse — toggling reveal fires an ordinary text-changed accessibility event carrying the real value as its before/after text, once per box, since none of these fields carry the isPassword marker that lets Compose recognise and suppress that event (see the Better version's developer note).

TODO(verify): confirm on a real device what TalkBack actually announces for that event on a plain, non-password field — this is the concrete shape of the "bullet bullet bullet replaced with 1 2 3" bug this topic is modelled on.

See the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.foundation.text.BasicSecureTextField

A plain vertical list — no grid, no table, just one column of items — has a position and a total that a screen reader can announce, like \"item 8 of 24\". Whether that announcement actually happens is not automatic, even though it looks like it should be.
Turn on TalkBack and swipe through the list below. Listen for whether TalkBack tells you your position in the list — \"item 3 of 24\" — or says nothing about position at all.

Both versions render this list with a plain LazyColumn — and LazyColumn already attaches CollectionInfo semantics to itself automatically, with no code from either version asking for it. That sounds like this topic should build itself. It doesn't: reading LazyLayoutSemanticState.kt directly shows the value it supplies is CollectionInfo(rowCount = -1, columnCount = 1) unconditionally — always "unknown", regardless of how many items are actually in the list, static or not. There are 24 fixed, fully-known items here, and LazyColumn's own default still reports the total as unknown.

This version overrides that default explicitly: Modifier.semantics { collectionInfo = CollectionInfo(rowCount = items.size, columnCount = 1) } layered onto the same LazyColumn. Confirmed by an instrumented test on a real device (Pixel 9 Pro, API 37, Compose BOM 2025.05.00), not just assumed from reading the API: this override is not merely plausible, it actually wins — the fetched semantics node reports the real count, not LazyColumn's internal -1. (The equivalent question for LazyVerticalGrid — where the internal default is arguably more actively misleading rather than just unhelpfully conservative — is still an open question in this project; see requirements §3.2.1 / Topic 7.)

Each item also carries its own CollectionItemInfo(rowIndex = index, …). This is never auto-supplied by any Lazy layout — confirmed by searching Compose Foundation's own source for every place it sets collectionItemInfo, which is nowhere. A collection container reporting a correct count does nothing for "item 8 of 24" without each item independently reporting which position it is.

TODO(verify): confirm the exact TalkBack announcement wording on a real device with TalkBack running — the source and the instrumented test confirm what semantics Compose exposes, not what TalkBack says out loud.

See: androidx.compose.foundation.lazy.LazyLayoutSemanticState, androidx.compose.ui.semantics.CollectionInfo, androidx.compose.ui.semantics.CollectionItemInfo

This list uses a plain LazyColumn with no accessibility code added at all — which might reasonably be assumed to mean TalkBack gets no positional information whatsoever. That is not quite what happens. LazyColumn attaches its own CollectionInfo semantics automatically (confirmed by reading LazyLayoutSemanticState.kt), so TalkBack does receive something — it is just always CollectionInfo(rowCount = -1, columnCount = 1), meaning "unknown", no matter how many items the list actually holds. These 24 items are fixed at composition; the real count is never in doubt. The default here is not a gap so much as a permanent, confident "I don't know" that a developer who never checked would have no reason to suspect.

Each item also carries no CollectionItemInfo of its own — nothing in Compose supplies that automatically for any Lazy layout, so "item 8 of 24" cannot be announced here even in principle, regardless of what the container reports.

See the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.foundation.lazy.LazyLayoutSemanticState

Some grids are genuinely two-dimensional — a column is not just a visual lane, it is a distinct field with its own meaning, like a price or a stock count next to a product name. Compose has no table composable at all; a table like this is built by hand out of ordinary rows and cells.

Turn on TalkBack and move through the table below, cell by cell. Listen for whether TalkBack ever relates a cell back to its row and column — does \"$9.99\" get tied to the product it belongs to, or is it just a number in a stream of unconnected text?

Compose has no table composable, so this grid is built by hand: a Column of Rows, each cell a Text. Unlike LazyColumn (see the One-Dimensional Collections topic), a plain Column supplies no CollectionInfo of its own — there is no framework default here to accidentally rely on, and nothing to override. It has to be added from scratch, on both the container and every cell.

This version adds Modifier.semantics { collectionInfo = CollectionInfo(rowCount = 6, columnCount = 3) } to the table's container, and a matching CollectionItemInfo(rowIndex, rowSpan, columnIndex, columnSpan) to every one of its 18 cells, including the header row. That per-cell information is what lets TalkBack relate a cell to the row and column it is actually in — "$9.99" means nothing on its own; "$9.99, row 2, column 2" ties it to whatever is in that row's first cell.

One honest limitation: CollectionItemInfo in this Compose version carries only position and span — rowIndex, rowSpan, columnIndex, columnSpan — with no separate flag marking a cell as a header, confirmed by reading its full constructor in SemanticsProperties.kt. The header row here is simply row 0; nothing in this API distinguishes it from a data row. TODO(verify): confirm on a real device whether TalkBack gives header-row cells any different treatment at all, since this API surface does not ask for it explicitly.

See: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.CollectionInfo, androidx.compose.ui.semantics.CollectionItemInfo

This is the same six-row, three-column grid, built the same way — a Column of Rows of Text cells, since Compose has no table composable. No CollectionInfo, no CollectionItemInfo, anywhere. Unlike the One-Dimensional Collections topic, there is no framework default quietly filling in a wrong-but-present value here either: a plain Column supplies nothing on its own, so this genuinely is silence, not a confidently wrong default.

TalkBack swipes through 18 individual text nodes with no indication that any of them relate to each other. "Widget", "$9.99", and "42" are three unconnected pieces of text in a stream, not a row — there is no way to tell, from what TalkBack announces, that the second cell is that first product's price rather than some unrelated number.

See the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.CollectionInfo

A contacts list grouped by first letter, with a pinned header for each letter that stays visible while its group scrolls past underneath it — a common real-world pattern for anything alphabetical, and one that is easy to get an accurate position count wrong for even with the best intentions.

Turn on TalkBack and swipe down through the contacts below, past several pinned letter headers. Listen for whether TalkBack ever announces your position among the contacts, and whether it can tell you moved from one letter\'s heading to the next.

This list is built from five separate stickyHeader()/items() block pairs, one per letter group — not a single items(count = N) call like the One-Dimensional Collections topic. That structural difference is the whole point of this topic: the itemContent lambda passed to items(count, …) { index -> … } does receive an index, but reading LazyLayoutIntervalContent.kt shows it is computed as val localIntervalIndex = globalIndex - interval.startIndex — local to that one items() call, resetting to 0 at the start of every letter group. Wiring that straight into CollectionItemInfo.rowIndex, the way a single-items()-call list safely can, would silently repeat positions from zero in every group after the first.

This version instead precomputes each contact's position across the whole flattened list before the LazyListScope body runs, so it stays correct no matter which stickyHeader()/items() block a given contact falls into. CollectionInfo.rowCount is likewise the real contact count only — 9, not the 14 a naive count of every emitted item (5 headers plus 9 contacts) would give.

Each header carries Modifier.semantics { heading() } for TalkBack's heading-navigation, but deliberately no CollectionItemInfo: this Compose version's CollectionItemInfo has no way to flag a row as a header at all (see the Genuine Tables topic), so a section header simply is not part of the row-index space here.

One fact worth knowing precisely because it looks similar and is not: stickyHeader() does receive a correct, framework-computed global index of its own. LazyListIntervalContent.kt shows headerIndex = intervals.size, captured at registration time — confirmed via IntervalList.kt, whose size is documented as the total item count across all intervals, not the number of interval calls. It is a real, correct index; it is just answering a different question than the one this topic's row index needs.

TODO(verify): confirm on a real device with TalkBack what a pinned sticky header does to positional announcements while it stays visually fixed at the top during a swipe past the contacts underneath it — the source above establishes what Compose reports, not what TalkBack does with it while a header is pinned.

See: androidx.compose.foundation.lazy.LazyDsl.kt, androidx.compose.foundation.lazy.layout.LazyLayoutIntervalContent.kt, androidx.compose.foundation.lazy.LazyListIntervalContent.kt, androidx.compose.foundation.lazy.layout.IntervalList.kt

This is the same five-group, nine-contact list, built the same way — stickyHeader() for each letter, items() for the contacts under it — with no accessibility semantics added anywhere. LazyColumn still attaches its own CollectionInfo automatically (see the One-Dimensional Collections topic), always as CollectionInfo(rowCount = -1, columnCount = 1) regardless of the real count, so the container reports "unknown" rather than 9. No item, header or contact, carries any CollectionItemInfo, since no Lazy layout ever supplies that on its own.

Even a well-intentioned attempt at a fix would be easy to get wrong here without knowing one specific fact: the index parameter delivered to items(count) { index -> … } is local to that one items() call, not a position in the whole list — reading LazyLayoutIntervalContent.kt confirms it is computed as the global index minus that call's own start position. This list is built from five separate stickyHeader()/items() pairs, so that index silently resets to 0 at the start of every letter group; wiring it directly into a row index, as a single-items()-call list can safely do, would produce wrong, repeating positions here rather than an honest "unknown".

The section headers also carry no heading() marking, so TalkBack's heading-navigation has no letter groups to jump between — a sighted user sees the alphabet structure at a glance; a TalkBack user gets nine contacts and five pinned labels in one undifferentiated swipe order.

See the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.foundation.lazy.LazyDsl.kt, androidx.compose.foundation.lazy.layout.LazyLayoutIntervalContent.kt
